newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam rallies state sector as trade gap widens.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam rallies state sector as trade gap widens.

text.p: Vietnam's leadership has urged the public sector to assert itself in foreign trade and has called for greater state control to beat smugglers, tax dodgers and counterfeiters, official dailies said on Wednesday.
The rallying call, from the inner Standing Board of the Politburo, came amid reports that the country's already alarming trade gap has widened to a new record.
The reports put the deficit for the first 11 months of this year at $3.71 billion, a leap from $2.3 billion for the whole of 1995 and equivalent to some 17 percent of annual national income.
Imports from the beginning of the year to the end of November were put at $10.18 billion and exports at $6.47 billion.

The Ha Noi Moi daily said the five-member Standing Board -- which includes the leadership triumvirate and two other members of the Politburo -- called on the state sector to take a lead in foreign trade.

"It is now necessary to focus on building state-owned enterprises which are able to play a leading role in multi-sector commerce," it said, adding that it was their job to manage trade in essential goods for production and consumption.

"The instruction clearly pointed out that it is necessary to reinforce state management and control over activities of the external economy, the market and trade activities of all economic sectors," it said.
Vietnam's roughly 6,000 state-owned enterprises dominate many sectors of the economy even though they yield only a quarter of the country's output and huge numbers of them are loss makers.

Although the Communist Party has pledged to level the playing field for both private and public sectors as part of continuing reforms, it wants the state sector to spearhead a drive for industrialisation and modernisation.

Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet recently issued a directive ordering closer management of non-state firms, ordering them to register or even re-register with the authorities to stamp out tax dodging, illegal business and dumping in the market.
The United Nations said in a recent report that the widening of the trade deficit could be partly linked to the country's system of tariffs, taxes, quotas and state monopoly powers.

"The...current set of incentives, regulations and systems for resource allocation appear to be impeding the development of Vietnam's employment-generating and export capacity, and risk promoting excessive imports for the development of uncompetitive industries and a high-cost economy," it said.
The report, "Catching Up", called for much deeper reform of state-owned enterprises, faster equitisation of state firms and the development of a healthy non-state sector.
